title: India's Gold Tariff Hike Was Supposed to Shrink the Trade Deficit. It Built a Smuggling Empire Instead.
excerpt: Illegal gold imports could hit 100 metric tons this year as grey-market discounts exceed $200 an ounce. Banks, refiners, and the legal market are caught in the crossfire.
body:
India raised gold import tariffs to curb demand and stem a widening trade deficit. On paper, it was textbook economic defence — make gold more expensive at the border, and fewer tonnes come in.

In practice, the policy has created one of the largest arbitrage opportunities in India's commodities market. Grey-market gold is now available at discounts exceeding $200 per ounce below legal channel prices. And smugglers, who had been retreating for years, are flooding back.

**The numbers tell the story.** Gold smuggling had fallen from 156.1 metric tons in 2023 to just 20.4 tons in 2025 after India slashed import duties. The reversal was dramatic — and it worked. Legal imports rose, tax revenue increased, and the illicit trade shrank to its lowest level in a decade.

Then the Iran war changed everything.

With the trade deficit ballooning — India's oil-and-gas import bill jumped 53% in April alone — Delhi reimposed steep tariffs on gold. The combined duty now sits at 18.45%, including import tariff and GST. The gap between what smugglers pay and what legal importers pay has turned gold into one of the most profitable contraband goods in the country.

Industry projections suggest illegal gold imports will exceed 100 metric tons in 2026. If that happens, the government stands to lose an estimated $2.65 billion in tariff and tax revenue — more than the deficit reduction the tariff hike was designed to achieve.

**The legal gold market is bleeding.** India imported 45.6 tons of gold in April through official channels. But imports may have halved in May, according to industry sources, as banks and refiners pulled back from overseas purchases. The reason is straightforward: smuggled gold is undercutting them.

Domestic discounts on legal gold now exceed $100 per ounce. At that level, refining imported gold dore — a semi-pure alloy that normally carries a 0.65% duty advantage — is uneconomical. "Gold refiners typically operate on margins of around 0.65%," says James Jose, managing director of refiner CGR Metalloys. "With discounts now well above that level, refiners have little incentive to import dore."

A Kolkata-based bullion dealer, speaking to Reuters, was blunter: the current spread between smuggled and legal gold is so wide that "anyone with the right connections is making a killing."

**For NRIs, the ripple effects are real.** Gold remains deeply embedded in Indian family life — weddings, festivals, savings. NRIs regularly buy gold during trips home or send money for family purchases. A booming grey market means the gold your family buys may not come with proper hallmarking, purity certification, or any recourse if something goes wrong. It also means jewellers who play by the rules are being squeezed out by those who don't.

The policy was meant to be a temporary wartime measure. But temporary measures in India have a habit of becoming permanent fixtures. And the longer the tariff stays at these levels, the deeper the smuggling networks entrench themselves — making any future rollback even harder.

Delhi is now caught in a familiar trap: the cure is feeding the disease. A tariff designed to protect the balance of payments is destroying the legal gold market that generates the tariff revenue in the first place.

The government has not signalled any plans to revisit the duty structure. Until it does, the grey market will keep growing, the legal market will keep shrinking, and India's gold trade will increasingly operate in the shadows — exactly where it was a decade ago, before years of reform pulled it into the light.

*Sources: Reuters, World Gold Council, Devdiscourse*
